content: The Quality Safety Manila, Philippines Guideline Development Group includes a diverse team of experts from various fields and regions. Among them: 1. Dr. Niveen Abu-Rmeileh, a professor at the Institute of Community and Public Health, Birzeit University, located in the occupied Palestinian territory, including East Jerusalem, specializes in community and public health as well as statistical epidemiology. She declared no conflicts of interest. 2. Professor Mario Festin, from the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology at the University of the Philippines College of Medicine in Manila, Philippines, has expertise in obstetrics, gynecology, clinical epidemiology, public health, and systematic reviews. He also declared no conflicts of interest. 3. Dr. Atf Ghérissi, an assistant professor at the Faculty of Health Sciences and Techniques, Tunis El Manar University, Tunisia, focuses on midwifery, systematic reviews, qualitative evidence, maternal and perinatal health, and community health. She reported no conflicts of interest. 4. Mrs. Gill Gyte, a consumer editor for the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group at Liverpool Women’s NHS Foundation Trust in the United Kingdom, represents consumer perspectives in pregnancy and childbirth. She declared no conflicts of interest. 5. Professor Tippawan Liabsuetrakul, head of the Epidemiology Unit at the Faculty of Medicine, Prince of Songkla University, Thailand, specializes in epidemiology, obstetrics, and gynecology. She reported no conflicts of interest. 6. Professor James Neilson, the chair of the Guideline Development Group and coordinating editor for the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group at Liverpool Women’s NHS Foundation Trust, United Kingdom, has expertise in general obstetrics, perinatology, gynecology, systematic reviews, evidence synthesis, and guideline development using the GRADE approach. He declared no conflicts of interest. 7. Dr. Lisa Noguchi, director of Maternal and Newborn Health at Jhpiego in Baltimore, Maryland, USA, focuses on midwifery, care delivery, and implementation science. She disclosed anticipated research funding from the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation related to innovations in antenatal and perinatal care. This conflict was deemed minor and did not affect her participation in the group. 8. Professor Nafissa Osman, an associate professor at Eduardo Mondlane University in Maputo, Mozambique, specializes in obstetrics, gynecology, and implementation research. She declared no conflicts of interest. 9. Professor Erika Ota, from St. Luke’s International University in Tokyo, Japan, focuses on midwifery, nutrition, evidence synthesis, and guideline development. She reported no conflicts of interest. 10. Dr. Tomas Pantoja, a professor at the Pontifical Catholic University of Chile in Santiago, specializes in family medicine, evidence synthesis, and health policy and programming. He declared no conflicts of interest. 11. Professor Robert Pattinson, director of the South African Medical Research Council/University of Pretoria Maternal and Infant Health Care Strategies Research Unit in South Africa, has expertise in obstetrics, gynecology, care delivery, and evidence synthesis. He reported no conflicts of interest. 12. Dr. Charlotte Warren, director of the Ending Eclampsia Project and senior associate in Maternal and Newborn Health at the Population Council in Washington, D.C., USA, specializes in nursing, maternal and perinatal health, health systems, policy and programming, and implementation research. She declared no conflicts of interest. 13. Professor Charles Shey Wiysonge, director of the South Africa Cochrane Centre at the South African Medical Research Council in Cape Town, South Africa, focuses on health systems, systematic reviews, and care delivery. He reported no conflicts of interest. The group also included systematic reviewers and methodologists, such as Professor Soo Downe (University of Central Lancashire, UK), Therese Dowswell (Evidence-Based Medicine Consultancy Ltd., UK), and Kenneth Finlayson (University of Central Lancashire, UK). Observers included Deborah Armbruster (USAID), Anwar Nassar (American University of Beirut, Lebanon), and Liona Poon (International Society of Ultrasound in Obstetrics and Gynecology, Hong Kong SAR). The group reviewed evidence on antenatal ultrasound before 24 weeks of gestation. Studies compared routine first-trimester scans (before 14 weeks) and second-trimester scans (14–24 weeks) with no routine scans. The findings included: Maternal Outcomes: Routine first-trimester scans showed low certainty of evidence, with 54 fewer adverse outcomes per 1,000 participants (ranging from 102 fewer to 18 more). Second-trimester scans showed very low certainty, with 42 fewer adverse outcomes per 1,000 participants (ranging from 46 fewer to 34 more). Fetal and Neonatal Outcomes: Routine first-trimester scans showed low certainty, with 37 more favorable outcomes per 1,000 participants (ranging from 0 fewer to 114 more). Second-trimester scans showed low certainty, with 27 more favorable outcomes per 1,000 participants (ranging from 5 fewer to 77 more). The evidence was limited by study design flaws, wide confidence intervals, and low event rates, which reduced the certainty of the findings.
